label: Possible side effects
summary: The game concept Possible Side Effects: the unexpected results a councillor task can have over time.
details: `[councillor_task_possible_side_effects|E]` in a text shows the words, linked to the concept's explanation. Side effects can be good or bad: good ones are likelier the higher the councillor's relevant skill, bad ones the lower it is. Vanilla uses it in the council task tooltip and a message filter.

label: Councillor task
summary: The plural name of the game concept Councillor Task: the jobs councillors can be given.
details: `[councillor_tasks|E]` in a text shows the plural, linked to the Councillor Task explanation. Vanilla uses it in AI personality texts, such as using council tasks to defend themselves.

label: Councillor
summary: The plural name of the game concept Councillor: a ruler's helpers on the council.
details: `[councillors|E]` in a text shows the plural, linked to the Councillor explanation. Vanilla uses it in requirements such as at least a number of councillors with some quality.

label: Count
summary: The game concept Count: a ruler whose primary title is a county.
details: `[count|E]` in a text shows the word Count, linked to the concept's explanation. A count ranks above barons and below dukes, so they can have barons as vassals and a duke or higher as liege.

label: Men-at-arms counter
summary: The game concept Men-at-Arms Counter: most kinds of men-at-arms are strong against (counter) another kind.
details: `[counter|E]` in a text shows the word Counter, linked to the concept's explanation. A countered regiment fights worse in battle, and the more it is outnumbered by the kind that counters it, the bigger the penalty. Vanilla uses it in the texts of each men-at-arms kind, such as skirmishers countering heavy infantry.

label: Men-at-arms counter
summary: Another name of the game concept Men-at-Arms Counter, written as counters (one kind of men-at-arms counters another).
details: `[counters|E]` in a text shows the word, linked to the explanation of countering: a countered regiment is less effective in battle. Vanilla uses it in the regiment tooltip listing the kinds a men-at-arms type counters.

label: County
summary: The plural name of the game concept County: the titles one tier below a duchy and one above a barony.
details: `[counties|E]` in a text shows the plural, linked to the County explanation. Vanilla uses it very often, for example in achievements about converting all counties of a region.

label: Count
summary: The plural name of the game concept Count: rulers whose primary title is a county.
details: `[counts|E]` in a text shows the plural, linked to the Count explanation. Vanilla uses it in a faction reason (counts want to stay vassals) and in the baron explanation.

label: County
summary: The game concept County: a title one tier below a duchy and one above a barony.
details: `[county|E]` in a text shows the word County, linked to the concept's explanation. The county title includes its county capital and the rightful (de jure) claim to all baronies in it. A county always has a holder, because a county capital cannot be destroyed.

label: County capital
summary: The game concept County Capital: the main holding of a county.
details: `[county_capital|E]` in a text shows the words, linked to the concept's explanation. It can never be destroyed or leased out, and always belongs to the ruler who holds the county title. It has room for one more building than a lesser holding.

label: County capital
summary: The plural name of the game concept County Capital: the main holdings of counties.
details: `[county_capitals|E]` in a text shows the plural, linked to the County Capital explanation. Vanilla's concept texts use it to say they cannot be leased and are always fortified.

label: County control
summary: The game concept County Control: how firmly the government holds the people of a county.
details: `[county_control|E]` in a text shows the words, linked to the concept's explanation. Control matters most for collecting taxes. It falls sharply when the county changes hands by war, and sieges and peasant uprisings damage it; low control can lead to county corruption. The marshal's council task is the main way to raise it.

label: County corruption
summary: The game concept County Corruption: negative county modifiers a county can get while its control is low or its holder is in debt.
details: `[county_corruption|E]` in a text shows the words, linked to the concept's explanation. Corruption fades over time but can come back while the cause (debt or low control) stays. The marshal's task to increase control clears it faster.

label: Development
summary: The game concept Development: how far a county's local infrastructure and technology have advanced.
details: `[county_development|E]` in a text shows the word Development, linked to the concept's explanation. Higher development gives the county more levies, taxes and supply limit.

label: Development growth
summary: The game concept Development Growth: a county's progress towards its next point of development.
details: `[county_development_growth|E]` in a text shows the words, linked to the concept's explanation. When growth reaches 100, the county's development goes up by 1. Vanilla's texts do not use this link.

label: County fertility
summary: The game concept County Fertility: the quality of a steppe county's pastures, which nomadic rulers graze to grow their herd.
details: `[county_fertility|E]` in a text shows the words, linked to the concept's explanation. It exists only in counties of the Great Steppe. Fertility settles around its equilibrium, changes with the steppe seasons and is slowly refilled by herders. Vanilla uses it in nomad council task texts.

label: County fertility icon
summary: The icon of the game concept County Fertility (the quality of a steppe county's pastures).
details: Written as a concept link, `[county_fertility_i|E]`, it shows the fertility icon linked to the explanation; vanilla writes it before a growth value in nomad council task texts.

label: County modifier
summary: The game concept County Modifier: a modifier that changes a county's values.
details: `[county_modifier|E]` in a text shows the words, linked to the concept's explanation. Baronies can have modifiers of their own, seen in the county's holdings. Vanilla uses it in a decision that removes a backwater modifier from developed counties.

label: County modifier
summary: The plural name of the game concept County Modifier: modifiers that change a county's values.
details: `[county_modifiers|E]` in a text shows the plural, linked to the County Modifier explanation. Vanilla uses it in the corruption explanation and in a diarchy interaction that gives negative ones to other vassals.

label: Popular opinion
summary: The game concept Popular Opinion: what the common people of a county think of the character who holds it.
details: `[county_opinion|E]` in a text shows the words Popular Opinion, linked to the concept's explanation. An unhappy population may start or join a peasant or popular faction, which can spread through a whole realm. The easiest way to keep it up is a holder of the people's culture and faith.

label: Court
summary: The game concept Court: the unlanded characters who serve a ruler.
details: `[court|E]` in a text shows the word Court, linked to the concept's explanation. Every ruler has one; it usually holds the ruler's family and a mix of useful nobles and commoners.

label: Court amenities
summary: The game concept Court Amenities: the standard of living a ruler sets in their royal court.
details: `[court_amenities|E]` in a text shows the words, linked to the concept's explanation. Each category (fashion, food, lodging and servants) has several levels, and spending more usually brings more court grandeur. Tribal rulers cannot choose the higher levels.

label: Court amenities
summary: The singular name of the game concept Court Amenities: one category of a royal court's living standard.
details: `[court_amenity|E]` in a text shows the singular, linked to the Court Amenities explanation. Vanilla uses it in texts that change an amenity's cost or upkeep, such as lodging upkeep.

label: Court artifact
summary: The game concept Court Artifact: an artifact displayed in a ruler's royal court, such as a tapestry or an illustrated book.
details: `[court_artifact|E]` in a text shows the words, linked to the concept's explanation. Court artifacts help decide the court's grandeur. A character can own any number, but only those in a display slot of their type have an effect. They come from inspired characters, the commission artifact decision and reforging.

label: Court artifact
summary: The plural name of the game concept Court Artifact: artifacts displayed in a royal court.
details: `[court_artifacts|E]` in a text shows the plural, linked to the Court Artifact explanation. Vanilla uses it in the royal court window and the royal court explanation.

label: Court chaplain
summary: The game concept Court Chaplain: the councillor in charge of religious matters in faiths with lay clergy.
details: `[court_chaplain|E]` in a text shows the words, linked to the concept's explanation. Faiths with temporal clergy have the stronger and more troublesome realm priest instead. Vanilla uses it in texts such as having no court chaplain.

label: Court chaplain
summary: The possessive name of the game concept Court Chaplain.
details: `[court_chaplain_possessive|E]` in a text shows the possessive, linked to the Court Chaplain explanation (the religious councillor in faiths with lay clergy). Vanilla uses it once, in a situation catalyst about a chaplain's replacement.

label: Court chaplain
summary: The plural name of the game concept Court Chaplain: the religious councillors of rulers in faiths with lay clergy.
details: `[court_chaplains|E]` in a text shows the plural, linked to the Court Chaplain explanation. Vanilla uses it in the clergy and realm priest explanations.

label: Court chaplain
summary: The plural possessive name of the game concept Court Chaplain, shown as Court Chaplains'.
details: `[court_chaplains_possessive|E]` in a text shows Court Chaplains', linked to the Court Chaplain explanation. Vanilla's texts do not use this form.

label: Court event
summary: The game concept Court Event: an event involving members of the ruler's court, viewed in the royal court.
details: `[court_event|E]` in a text shows the words, linked to the concept's explanation. Vanilla's texts use the plural form instead.

label: Court event
summary: The plural name of the game concept Court Event: events involving members of the ruler's court.
details: `[court_events|E]` in a text shows the plural, linked to the Court Event explanation. Vanilla uses it in the trigger texts for having, or not having, pending court events.

label: Court grandeur
summary: The game concept Court Grandeur: how famous a royal court is, a value from 0 to 100 that unlocks grandeur levels.
details: `[court_grandeur|E]` in a text shows the words, linked to the concept's explanation. Over time the value settles at its baseline, which dynasty perks, amenity spending and magnificent court artifacts raise. Part of it is lost on succession.

label: Court grandeur expectations
summary: The singular name of the game concept Court Grandeur Expectations: the grandeur level a ruler's realm size calls for.
details: `[court_grandeur_expectation|E]` in a text shows the singular, linked to the expectations explanation. Vanilla uses it once, in the court grandeur window's current expected level.

label: Court grandeur expectations
summary: The game concept Court Grandeur Expectations: the court grandeur level a ruler is expected to reach for the size of their realm.
details: `[court_grandeur_expectations|E]` in a text shows the words, linked to the concept's explanation. The larger the realm, the grander the court must be. Falling short brings penalties, going beyond brings bonuses. For tribal rulers the expectation always equals their current level. Vanilla uses it in a faction reason when the liege is below expectations.

label: Court grandeur level
summary: The game concept Court Grandeur Level: a level of a royal court's grandeur that gives its owner bonuses.
details: `[court_grandeur_level|E]` in a text shows the words, linked to the concept's explanation. Levels unlock as the court's grandeur value rises, and large realms are expected to reach higher levels.

label: Court grandeur level
summary: The plural name of the game concept Court Grandeur Level.
details: `[court_grandeur_levels|E]` in a text shows the plural, linked to the Court Grandeur Level explanation (levels of a court's grandeur that give bonuses). Vanilla uses it in texts such as a court being two levels above what is expected.

label: Court grandeur
summary: Another name of the game concept Court Grandeur: the value (0 to 100) of how famous a royal court is.
details: `[court_grandeur_value|E]` in a text shows the word, linked to the Court Grandeur explanation. Vanilla's concept texts use it for the value that unlocks grandeur levels and that amenity spending raises.

label: Court guest
summary: The game concept Court Guest: a wanderer who stays at a court for a limited time.
details: `[court_guest|E]` in a text shows the words, linked to the concept's explanation. The ruler can recruit a guest as a permanent courtier. Vanilla's texts do not use this link.

label: Court host
summary: The game concept Court Host: a ruler who has a character in their court without being that character's liege.
details: `[court_host|E]` in a text shows the words, linked to the concept's explanation. This happens, for example, when wanderers visit a ruler or a ward lives at their guardian's court. Vanilla's texts do not use this link.

label: Court language
summary: The game concept Court Language: the official language of a royal court, spoken by its nobles and used by its officials.
details: `[court_language|E]` in a text shows the words, linked to the concept's explanation. The court grandeur baseline rises for each county of the realm sharing the language, for each royal court with the same court language, and when it is the ruler's native language.

label: Court language
summary: The plural name of the game concept Court Language.
details: `[court_languages|E]` in a text shows the plural, linked to the Court Language explanation (the official language of a royal court). Vanilla uses it in the court languages map mode.

label: Court position
summary: The game concept Court Position: a special role a liege can give a courtier or vassal so they help the liege.
details: `[court_position|E]` in a text shows the words, linked to the concept's explanation. The benefits depend on the holder's aptitude for the position. Granting one is free, but it has a monthly gold salary, and revoking it costs prestige.

label: Court position icon
summary: The icon of the game concept Court Position (a special role in a ruler's court).
details: `[court_position_i]` in a text shows the court position icon; vanilla writes it before the words excellent-aptitude court positions in lists of bonuses.

label: Court position task
summary: The game concept Court Position Task: an extra task some court positions can perform, often giving more benefits at an extra cost.
details: `[court_position_task|E]` in a text shows the words, linked to the concept's explanation. Each court position can have only one task active at a time.

label: Court position task
summary: The short name of the game concept Court Position Task, shown as the word Task.
details: `[court_position_task_short|E]` in a text shows Task, linked to the Court Position Task explanation. Vanilla uses it in the court position window, such as the task cost breakdown.

label: Court position task
summary: The plural name of the game concept Court Position Task.
details: `[court_position_tasks|E]` in a text shows the plural, linked to the Court Position Task explanation (extra tasks some court positions can perform). Vanilla uses it in trait and epidemic texts naming tasks of certain positions.

label: Court position task
summary: The short plural name of the game concept Court Position Task, shown as the word Tasks.
details: `[court_position_tasks_short|E]` in a text shows Tasks, linked to the Court Position Task explanation. Vanilla uses it in the hint listing a position's possible tasks.

label: Court position
summary: The plural name of the game concept Court Position: the special roles in a ruler's court.
details: `[court_positions|E]` in a text shows the plural, linked to the Court Position explanation. Vanilla uses it in the court positions window, such as no one being eligible.

label: Court type
summary: The game concept Court Type: the kind of royal court a ruler has chosen, each with its own bonuses.
details: `[court_type|E]` in a text shows the words, linked to the concept's explanation. A court type's bonuses for the ruler and court depend on the court grandeur level. The ethos of the ruler's culture decides which types they can choose.

label: Court type trait
summary: The game concept Court Type Trait: a trait a courtier gets after serving some years in a royal court, matching that court's type.
details: `[court_type_trait|E]` in a text shows the words, linked to the concept's explanation. How good the trait is depends on how long the character has served in that court. The number of years comes from a script value (`years_to_gain_court_type_trait`).

label: Court type
summary: The plural name of the game concept Court Type.
details: `[court_types|E]` in a text shows the plural, linked to the Court Type explanation (the kinds of royal court with their own bonuses). Vanilla uses it once, in a tutorial text.

label: Courtier
summary: The game concept Courtier: an unlanded character who serves a ruler in their court.
details: `[courtier|E]` in a text shows the word Courtier, linked to the concept's explanation. Courtiers can be councillors, hold court positions, command armies or serve as knights, become vassals when given a title, and let the ruler press their claims in war. Adventurers have followers instead of courtiers.

label: Courtier
summary: The plural name of the game concept Courtier: the unlanded characters serving a ruler.
details: `[courtiers|E]` in a text shows the plural, linked to the Courtier explanation. Vanilla uses it in requirements such as at least a number of courtiers with some quality.

label: Court
summary: The plural name of the game concept Court: the groups of characters serving rulers.
details: `[courts|E]` in a text shows the plural, linked to the Court explanation. Vanilla uses it in tutorial and cultural tradition texts.

label: Terrified
summary: The game concept Terrified: a character so afraid of another that they will rarely act against them.
details: `[cowed|E]` in a text shows the word Terrified, linked to the concept's explanation. A terrified character avoids hostile actions against the one they fear, joining factions included. Dread and a cowardly personality make characters terrified or intimidated.

label: Title creation
summary: Another name of the game concept Title Creation, shown as the verb Create.
details: `[create|E]` in a text shows Create, linked to the Title Creation explanation: a ruler who controls most of a title's rightful (de jure) land that does not exist yet can create it, paying gold and gaining prestige. Vanilla uses it in the important actions about titles that can be created.

label: Title creation
summary: Another name of the game concept Title Creation, shown as the words Create Title.
details: `[create_title|E]` in a text shows Create Title, linked to the Title Creation explanation. Only duchies, kingdoms and empires can be created. Vanilla's texts do not use this form.

label: Title creation
summary: Another name of the game concept Title Creation, written as created (a title that has been created).
details: `[created|E]` in a text shows the word, linked to the Title Creation explanation. Vanilla uses it once, in a concept text saying higher titles can be created by a ruler who controls enough of their land.

label: Title creation
summary: Another name of the game concept Title Creation, shown as the words Created Title.
details: `[created_title|E]` in a text shows Created Title, linked to the Title Creation explanation. The one vanilla line found writes `[created_title.GetNameNoTierNoTooltip]`, which reads as a saved title of the same name in an event, not this concept.

label: Crime
summary: The game concept Crime: an act society finds bad enough to punish.
details: `[crime|E]` in a text shows the word Crime, linked to the concept's explanation. Secular crimes (such as a vassal revolting against their liege) can only be punished by those harmed; religious crimes (behaviour the faith's doctrines forbid) can be punished by any ruler over their subjects. Every crime lets a ruler imprison the criminal, and the worse ones allow revoking titles, banishment, torture or execution. Each crime can be punished only once per ruler.

label: Crime icon
summary: The icon of the game concept Crime (an act worthy of punishment).
details: `[crime_i]` in a text shows the crime icon; vanilla writes it at the start of trait texts saying something is a crime to a character.

label: Crime
summary: The plural name of the game concept Crime.
details: `[crimes|E]` in a text shows the plural, linked to the Crime explanation (acts worthy of punishment). Vanilla uses it in important actions about subjects whose crimes allow imprisoning them without tyranny.

label: Crime
summary: Another name of the game concept Crime, shown as the word Criminal (someone who committed a crime, or something considered a crime).
details: `[criminal|E]` in a text shows Criminal, linked to the Crime explanation. Vanilla uses it often, for example in faction reasons for traits considered criminal.

label: Criminal contract
summary: The game concept Criminal Contract: a shady task contract for adventurers that may pay well but gives experience in the gallowsbait trait.
details: `[criminal_task_contract|E]` in a text shows the words Criminal Contract, linked to the concept's explanation. Raising the gallowsbait trait makes most of the world hate and respect the adventurer less, and in time followers who dislike the banditry leave. Vanilla uses it in perk and contract texts, such as doubled gold rewards from criminal contracts.

label: Criminal contract
summary: The possessive name of the game concept Criminal Contract, shown as Criminal Contract's.
details: `[criminal_task_contract_possessive|E]` in a text shows Criminal Contract's, linked to the explanation of criminal contracts. Vanilla's texts do not use this form.

label: Criminal contract
summary: The plural name of the game concept Criminal Contract: shady task contracts for adventurers.
details: `[criminal_task_contracts|E]` in a text shows the plural, linked to the Criminal Contract explanation. Vanilla uses it in a camp purpose that finds more of them and in the contractor explanation.

label: Criminal contract
summary: The plural possessive name of the game concept Criminal Contract.
details: `[criminal_task_contracts_possessive|E]` in a text shows the plural possessive, linked to the explanation of criminal contracts (shady task contracts that give gallowsbait experience). Vanilla's texts do not use this form.

label: Crime
summary: Another name of the game concept Crime, shown as the word Criminals (characters who committed crimes).
details: `[criminals|E]` in a text shows the word, linked to the Crime explanation. Vanilla uses it in AI personality texts about punishing or pardoning criminals.

label: Critical failure
summary: The game concept Critical Failure: a bad outcome some schemes can have while they are carried out.
details: `[critical_failure|E]` in a text shows the words, linked to the concept's explanation. Outcomes vary: the scheme may backfire on its owner, or the owner may be barred for a while from trying the same scheme on the same target. Vanilla's texts use the verb form instead.

label: Critical failure
summary: Another name of the game concept Critical Failure, written as the verb critically fail.
details: `[critically_fail|E]` in a text shows the verb, linked to the Critical Failure explanation (a scheme backfiring or blocking a retry). Vanilla uses it in effect texts saying a character can no longer critically fail seduction schemes.

label: Crown authority
summary: The game concept Crown Authority: how much power a ruler has over their vassals.
details: `[crown_authority|E]` in a text shows the words, linked to the concept's explanation. There are four levels: autonomous vassals, limited, high and absolute. Raising it costs prestige, depending on the level and the ruler's learning skill. Vassals dislike higher levels, and lowering it is the main goal of the liberty faction.

label: Undirected great holy war
summary: Another name of the game concept Undirected Great Holy War, shown as the word Crusade.
details: `[crusade|E]` in a text shows Crusade, linked to the explanation of the great holy war a spiritual head of faith declares to bring a kingdom under their faith. It first goes through a preparation phase, during which rulers of the attacking faith can give gold to the war chest. Vanilla uses it in game rule texts about the first Catholic crusade.

label: Undirected great holy war
summary: Another name of the game concept Undirected Great Holy War, shown as the word Crusades.
details: `[crusades|E]` in a text shows Crusades, linked to the explanation of great holy wars declared by a head of faith. Vanilla uses it once, in a game rule text counting the Catholic crusades needed first.

label: Crush
summary: The game concept Crush: another child for whom a child develops their first feelings.
details: `[crush|E]` in a text shows the word Crush, linked to the concept's explanation. When they grow up, a mutual crush may turn into lovers, or the character moves on. Vanilla uses it in effect texts such as developing a crush on someone.

label: Crush
summary: The possessive name of the game concept Crush, shown as Crush's.
details: `[crush_possessive|E]` in a text shows Crush's, linked to the explanation of a child's first feelings for another child. Vanilla's texts do not use this form.

label: Crush
summary: The plural name of the game concept Crush.
details: `[crushes|E]` in a text shows the plural, linked to the Crush explanation (a child's first feelings for another child). Vanilla uses it once, in the trigger text comparing the number of crushes.

label: Crush
summary: The plural possessive name of the game concept Crush, shown as Crushes'.
details: `[crushes_possessive|E]` in a text shows Crushes', linked to the Crush explanation. Vanilla's texts do not use this form.

label: Culture
summary: Another name of the game concept Culture, shown as the word Cultural.
details: `[cultural|E]` in a text shows Cultural, linked to the Culture explanation (the language and customs of a character or county). Vanilla uses it in texts such as a shared cultural heritage or cultural men-at-arms.

label: Cultural acceptance
summary: The game concept Cultural Acceptance: how accepting two cultures are of each other.
details: `[cultural_acceptance|E]` in a text shows the words, linked to the concept's explanation. It mainly sets how much opinion drops between characters of different cultures; it also affects popular opinion and the cost of forming a hybrid culture. Wars, granting and revoking titles and the accept culture council task change it, and over time it returns to its baseline when above it.

label: Cultural acceptance baseline
summary: The game concept Cultural Acceptance Baseline: the level that cultural acceptance falls back to when it is higher.
details: `[cultural_acceptance_baseline|E]` in a text shows the words, linked to the concept's explanation. The baseline depends on what two cultures share: heritage, language, faith and religion (more so with pluralistic or eastern faiths), and ethos within the same region.

label: Cultural acceptance icon
summary: The icon of the game concept Cultural Acceptance (how accepting two cultures are of each other).
details: `[cultural_acceptance_i]` in a text shows the cultural acceptance icon; vanilla writes it before a value in nomad council task texts about culture hybridizing.

label: Cultural fascination
summary: The game concept Cultural Fascination: the innovation a culture is focused on, which it discovers much faster.
details: `[cultural_fascination|E]` in a text shows the words, linked to the concept's explanation. The speed depends on the culture head's skills, each innovation benefiting from one skill. The culture head can change the fascination freely.

label: Cultural festival
summary: The game concept Cultural Festival: a phase of a royal tour in which a vassal entertains their liege.
details: `[cultural_festival|E]` in a text shows the words, linked to the concept's explanation. It often raises popular opinion and cultural acceptance.

label: Cultural festival
summary: The plural name of the game concept Cultural Festival.
details: `[cultural_festivals|E]` in a text shows the plural, linked to the Cultural Festival explanation (a royal tour phase where a vassal entertains their liege). Vanilla's texts do not use this form.

label: Culture head
summary: Another name of the game concept Culture Head: the ruler with the most influence over their culture.
details: `[cultural_head|E]` in a text shows the word, linked to the Culture Head explanation. The culture head is the ruler with the most counties of their own culture in their realm, wherever their domain is. Vanilla uses it in the culture window, such as the fascination marker.

label: Cultural spread
summary: The game concept Cultural Spread: contact with other cultures that know an innovation speeds up its discovery.
details: `[cultural_spread|E]` in a text shows the words, linked to the concept's explanation. Among the eligible cultures, the one with the highest cultural acceptance is chosen to spread its innovation progress. Vanilla's texts do not use this link.

label: Culture
summary: The game concept Culture: the language and customs of a character or a county.
details: `[culture|E]` in a text shows the word Culture, linked to the concept's explanation. Characters of different cultures have lower opinions of each other; more cultural acceptance reduces that penalty.

label: Cultural festival
summary: Another name of the game concept Cultural Festival, shown as the words Culture Festival.
details: `[culture_festival|E]` in a text shows Culture Festival, linked to the explanation of the royal tour phase where a vassal entertains their liege. Vanilla's texts do not use this form.

label: Cultural festival
summary: The game concept Cultural Festival: a stage of a royal tour in which a vassal is expected to entertain their liege.
details: This is another name of the cultural festival concept; writing `[culture_festivals|E]` in a text shows the word linked to its explanation. Such a festival often raises county opinion (how the county's people feel about their ruler) and cultural acceptance. The base game's texts do not use this key.

label: Culture head
summary: The game concept Culture Head: the ruler with the most influence over their own culture.
details: Writing `[culture_head|E]` in a text shows the word linked to the concept's explanation. The culture head is the ruler whose realm holds the most counties of that culture, wherever their own domain lies. Vanilla's texts say the culture head can change some cultural pillars and traditions through reformation.

label: Culture icon
summary: The game concept Culture (the language and customs of a character or county), in its `_i` form.
details: This is one of the culture concept's other names. Vanilla writes it as `[culture_i]` on its own, without `|E`, right before a number, which suggests it shows the concept's icon (the concept has one) rather than a word. Characters of different cultures like each other less; cultural acceptance reduces that penalty.

label: Culture intermingling
summary: The game concept Culture Intermingling: two cultures living side by side in one realm slowly come to accept each other.
details: Writing `[culture_intermingling|E]` in a text shows the word linked to the concept's explanation. The more of both cultures there is in the same realm, the more they intermingle, and that raises their cultural acceptance of each other.

label: Cultural pillar
summary: The game concept Cultural Pillar: one of the basic qualities that reflect where a culture comes from.
details: Writing `[culture_pillar|E]` in a text shows the word linked to the concept's explanation. The five pillars are ethos, heritage, language, martial custom and aesthetics. With the culture reform feature, the culture head can change ethos, language and martial custom through reformation; without it, the pillars cannot change.

label: Cultural pillars
summary: The game concept Cultural Pillar in its plural form: the basic qualities that reflect where a culture comes from.
details: Writing `[culture_pillars|E]` in a text shows the plural word linked to the concept's explanation. The pillars are ethos, heritage, language, martial custom and aesthetics. Vanilla uses it in texts about hybrid cultures, which mix the pillars of two cultures.

label: Culture's
summary: The game concept Culture (the language and customs of a character or county), in its possessive form.
details: Writing `[culture_possessive|E]` in a text shows the possessive word linked to the culture concept's explanation, as in vanilla's "Your culture's traditions change". Characters of different cultures like each other less; cultural acceptance reduces that penalty.

label: Cultural tradition
summary: The game concept Cultural Tradition: a practice, habit or value of a culture that gives its characters or counties a bonus or special ability.
details: Writing `[culture_tradition|E]` in a text shows the word linked to the concept's explanation. A culture can have up to 6 traditions, most have fewer. With the culture reform feature, the culture head can add or replace traditions through reformation.

label: Cultural traditions
summary: The game concept Cultural Tradition in its plural form: the practices and values of a culture that give bonuses or special abilities.
details: Writing `[culture_traditions|E]` in a text shows the plural word linked to the concept's explanation. A culture can have up to 6 traditions. Vanilla's texts mention, for example, traditions that lower the dangers of travel.

label: Cultures
summary: The game concept Culture in its plural form: the languages and customs of characters and counties.
details: Writing `[cultures|E]` in a text shows the plural word linked to the culture concept's explanation. Characters of different cultures like each other less; cultural acceptance reduces that penalty.

label: Damage
summary: The game concept Damage: how many casualties a soldier can inflict on the enemy in battle.
details: Writing `[damage|E]` in a text shows the word linked to the concept's explanation. The concept text gives a levy soldier's damage from the game's combat settings. Vanilla also uses it for men-at-arms and for the damage knights get from prowess.

label: De jure
summary: The game concept De Jure ("by law"): which higher title a title legally belongs to.
details: Writing `[de_jure|E]` in a text shows the word linked to the concept's explanation. A realm may not yet hold all the lands that legally belong to its title. The holder of a duchy, kingdom or empire always has a reason for war (casus belli) to take its de jure parts, and vassals judge who their rightful liege is by it.

label: De jure capital
summary: The game concept De Jure Capital: the county that was a title's historical capital.
details: Writing `[de_jure_capital|E]` in a text shows the word linked to the concept's explanation. A ruler can always move their realm capital to their primary title's de jure capital, even if it was moved before. Vanilla uses it in the decision to set a new de jure capital.

label: De jure drift
summary: The game concept De Jure Drift: the slow process by which a title comes to legally belong to a different higher title.
details: Writing `[de_jure_drift|E]` in a text shows the word linked to the concept's explanation. It happens when a duchy or kingdom lies entirely in the realm of a ruler who does not hold its de jure liege title. Duchies drift only into kingdoms and kingdoms only into empires. The chancellor's council task speeds it up.

label: Drift (de jure)
summary: The game concept De Jure Drift, in the form of the verb "drift".
details: Writing `[de_jure_drift_drift|E]` in a text shows the verb linked to the de jure drift explanation, as in vanilla's text on partitioned realms, which can drift duchies from one title into the other. De jure drift is the slow process by which a title comes to legally belong to a different higher title.

label: Drifted (de jure)
summary: The game concept De Jure Drift, in the form "drifted".
details: Writing `[de_jure_drift_drifted|E]` in a text shows the word linked to the de jure drift explanation, as in vanilla's "it will be drifted into Aragon". De jure drift is the slow process by which a title comes to legally belong to a different higher title.

label: Drifting (de jure)
summary: The game concept De Jure Drift, in the form "drifting".
details: Writing `[de_jure_drifting|E]` in a text shows the word linked to the de jure drift explanation; vanilla uses it in the trigger texts "is drifting towards". De jure drift is the slow process by which a title comes to legally belong to a different higher title.

label: De jure partition
summary: The game concept De Jure Partition: a realm split into two titles of the same tier that can still be reunited easily.
details: Writing `[de_jure_partition|E]` in a text shows the word linked to the concept's explanation. Either title can take fully controlled duchies of the other into its de jure lands at once through a decision. If one of the two is destroyed or loses its last de jure county, the other takes over the rest.

label: De jure partitioned
summary: The game concept De Jure Partition, in the form "partitioned".
details: Writing `[de_jure_partitioned|E]` in a text shows the word linked to the partition explanation; vanilla uses it for England and the Danelaw. A partitioned realm is split into two titles of the same tier that can still be reunited easily, for example by moving fully controlled duchies between them through a decision.

label: Fatal casualties
summary: The game concept Fatal Casualties: soldiers killed or wounded too badly to fight again in a battle.
details: Writing `[dead_soldiers|E]` in a text shows the word linked to the concept's explanation. These are permanent losses, unlike routed soldiers, who return to the army after the battle.

label: Death in combat
summary: The game concept Combat as a kind of death: dying from a blow in battle, a duel or another martial contest such as a tournament.
details: Writing `[death_combat|E]` in a text shows the word linked to the concept's explanation. Vanilla uses it in texts listing which kinds of death are acceptable, for example for a house's aspects.

label: Death by murder
summary: The game concept Murder as a kind of death: being murdered.
details: Writing `[death_murder|E]` in a text shows the word linked to the concept's explanation. Vanilla uses it in texts listing which kinds of death are acceptable, for example for the Aspect of Trickery.

label: Natural causes
summary: The game concept Natural Causes as a kind of death: dying peacefully, mainly of old age or long illness.
details: This is another name of the natural causes concept; writing `[death_natural_cause|E]` in a text shows the word linked to its explanation. Vanilla uses it in texts listing the only kinds of death a character may die from.

label: Natural causes
summary: The game concept Natural Causes as a kind of death: dying peacefully, mainly of old age or long illness.
details: Writing `[death_natural_causes|E]` in a text shows the word linked to the concept's explanation. Vanilla uses it in texts listing which kinds of death are acceptable for a house's aspects.

label: Religious death
summary: The game concept Religion as a kind of death: being killed for one's faith, such as martyrdom.
details: Writing `[death_religion|E]` in a text shows the word linked to the concept's explanation. Vanilla uses it in texts listing which kinds of death are acceptable for a house's aspects.

label: Religious death
summary: The game concept Religion as a kind of death: being killed for one's faith, such as martyrdom.
details: This is another name of the religious death concept; writing `[death_religious|E]` in a text shows the word linked to its explanation. Vanilla uses it in texts listing the only kinds of death a character may die from.

label: Debt
summary: The game concept Debt: having a negative amount of gold.
details: Writing `[debt|E]` in a text shows the word linked to the concept's explanation. A ruler in debt cannot declare new wars, their men-at-arms do not refill and enemies get an advantage in battle. The deeper the debt, the more penalties follow, such as fewer levies and lower county opinion.

label: Test loyalty value
summary: A game concept named Test Loyalty Value, used by the game's debug test story; its text speaks of a loyalty meter going up or down.
details: Writing `[debug_test_story|E]` in a text shows the word linked to the concept's explanation. Vanilla uses it only in the texts of its debug story test event, so it looks like a test item, not part of normal play. The concept text itself is unclear.

label: Study the Art of Scheming
summary: The game concept for the decision "Study the Art of Scheming", which improves the character's hostile schemes.
details: Writing `[deceitful_progress_hostile_schemes_decision|E]` in a text shows the decision's name linked to the concept's explanation. The decision gives success chance and scheme speed and costs stress. Vanilla's trait texts say a trait unlocks it.

label: Decide
summary: The game concept Decision, in the form of the verb "decide".
details: Writing `[decide|E]` in a text shows the verb linked to the decision concept's explanation, as in vanilla's "rulers can decide to make a Vow of Poverty". A decision is a special action a character can take whenever they like.

label: Decision
summary: The game concept Decision: a special action a character can take whenever they like.
details: Writing `[decision|E]` in a text shows the word linked to the concept's explanation. Each decision has its own effects, from small changes to the character up to ones that shake empires. Decisions that send a character somewhere for a while are called activities.

label: Decisions
summary: The game concept Decision in its plural form: special actions a character can take whenever they like.
details: Writing `[decisions|E]` in a text shows the plural word linked to the decision concept's explanation. Each decision has its own effects; ones that send a character somewhere for a while are called activities.

label: Mandala decree
summary: The game concept Mandala Decree: one of the three decrees a mandala ruler sets, for prosperity, expansion or reverence.
details: This is another name of the mandala decree concept; writing `[decree|E]` in a text shows the word linked to its explanation. A mandala realm is strongly centralized, with power over subjects and laws in the ruler's hands.

label: Mandala decrees
summary: The game concept Mandala Decree in its plural form: the three decrees a mandala ruler sets, for prosperity, expansion and reverence.
details: Writing `[decrees|E]` in a text shows the plural word linked to the mandala decree explanation. A mandala realm is strongly centralized, with power over subjects and laws in the ruler's hands.

label: Defeat
summary: The game concept Defeat: one of the three ways a war can end in a peace offer, with one side losing.
details: Writing `[defeat|E]` in a text shows the word linked to the concept's explanation. What a defeat costs depends on the reason for the war (casus belli). Defeated defenders usually lose titles in the war's target region; defeated attackers instead lose things like gold, prestige and piety.

label: Demand conversion
summary: The game concept Demand Conversion: a ruler asks a subject of another faith to take up the ruler's faith.
details: Writing `[demand_conversion|E]` in a text shows the word linked to the concept's explanation. Whether the subject accepts depends mostly on the ruler's learning skill and the subject's opinion of their liege; the concept text links a refusal to a crime concept.

label: Demand payment
summary: The game concept Demand Payment: a diplomatic interaction to demand gold from a character the actor has a hook on, in exchange for the hook.
details: Writing `[demand_payment|E]` in a text shows the word linked to the concept's explanation.

label: Demand payment
summary: The game concept Demand Payment: a diplomatic interaction to demand gold from a character the actor has a hook on, in exchange for the hook.
details: This is another name of the demand payment concept; writing `[demand_payment_decision|E]` in a text shows the word linked to its explanation. Vanilla uses it in a struggle text that unlocks demanding payment from rulers involved in the struggle.

label: Demanding conversion
summary: The game concept Demand Conversion, in the form "demanding conversion".
details: Writing `[demanding_conversion|E]` in a text shows the words linked to the demand conversion explanation. Demand Conversion is a ruler asking a subject of another faith to take up the ruler's faith; the ruler's learning and the subject's opinion decide the answer.

label: Denounce
summary: The game concept Denounce: a dynasty head publicly denounces a member of their dynasty, paying dynasty prestige.
details: Writing `[denounce|E]` in a text shows the word linked to the concept's explanation. Every member of the dynasty, the head included, then has a reason to imprison the denounced member.

label: Denouncement
summary: The game concept Denounce, in the noun form "denouncement".
details: Writing `[denouncement|E]` in a text shows the word linked to the denounce explanation. A dynasty head can denounce a member of their dynasty for dynasty prestige; all dynasty members then have a reason to imprison that member.

label: Depose
summary: The game concept Depose: a ruler is removed from power while still alive, as a faction demand or through special events.
details: Writing `[depose|E]` in a text shows the word linked to the concept's explanation. The deposed ruler's heirs inherit their titles as if the ruler had died.

label: Deposed
summary: The game concept Depose, in the form "deposed".
details: Writing `[deposed|E]` in a text shows the word linked to the depose explanation. A deposed ruler loses power while alive, through a faction's demands or special events, and their heirs inherit their titles.

label: Designate chief sacrifice
summary: The game concept Designate Chief Sacrifice: at a grand sacrificial festival, the host picks one of their prisoners as the main sacrifice.
details: Writing `[designate_chief_sacrifice|E]` in a text shows the word linked to the concept's explanation. That prisoner is killed first and can earn the host more piety. The concept text also lists which prisoners make better sacrifices.

label: Designate a chief sacrifice
summary: The game concept Designate Chief Sacrifice, in a form used inside a sentence.
details: Writing `[designate_chief_sacrifice_article|E]` in a text shows "Designate a Chief Sacrifice" linked to the concept's explanation, as in vanilla's "you may designate a chief sacrifice from among your prisoners". The chosen prisoner is killed first at a grand sacrificial festival and can earn more piety.

label: Chief sacrifice
summary: The game concept Designate Chief Sacrifice, in the noun form "chief sacrifice": the prisoner picked as the main sacrifice.
details: Writing `[designate_chief_sacrifice_chief_sacrifice|E]` in a text shows the words linked to the concept's explanation, as in vanilla's "Select ... as your personal chief sacrifice". That prisoner is killed first at a grand sacrificial festival and can earn the host more piety.

label: Designated heir
summary: The game concept Designated Heir: a character who comes first when the game decides who becomes the realm's heir.
details: Writing `[designated_heir|E]` in a text shows the word linked to the concept's explanation.

label: Designated terrain
summary: The game concept Designated Terrain: a decision from the wanderer lifestyle tree that picks one terrain group to specialize in.
details: Writing `[designated_terrain|E]` in a text shows the word linked to the concept's explanation. Some perks then give different bonuses for the chosen terrain group, such as forests and jungles.

label: Destination
summary: The game concept Destination: the place, or one of the places, a traveling character is heading for.
details: Writing `[destination|E]` in a text shows the word linked to the concept's explanation. For a pilgrimage it is the holy site; for a tour every vassal visited counts as a destination.

label: Details map
summary: The game concept Details Map: the closest map zoom level, which shows terrain and the player's domain.
details: Writing `[detail_zoom|E]` in a text shows the name linked to the concept's explanation. The game's tooltip says it suits moving regiments and building, and clicking the map there selects holdings. Vanilla lists it with the political and paper zoom levels.

label: Increase development in county
summary: The game concept for the steward's council task "Increase Development in County".
details: Writing `[develop_county|E]` in a text shows the task's name linked to the concept's explanation. The task targets one county, speeds up its development growth and shortens the building time of its buildings.

label: Development
summary: The game concept Development: how advanced a county's local infrastructure and technology are.
details: This is another name of the county development concept; writing `[development|E]` in a text shows the word linked to its explanation. Higher development gives more levies, taxes and supply limit from the county.

label: Development growth
summary: The game concept Development Growth: how far a county has come towards its next point of development.
details: Writing `[development_growth|E]` in a text shows the word linked to the concept's explanation. At 100 growth the county's development rises by 1.

label: Development icon
summary: The game concept Development (how advanced a county's infrastructure and technology are), in its `_i` form.
details: This is one of the county development concept's other names. Vanilla writes it as `[development_i]` without `|E`, right before a number or the linked word, which suggests it shows the concept's icon. Higher development gives more levies, taxes and supply limit.

label: Diarch
summary: The game concept Diarch: the junior partner who helps their liege run the realm during power sharing.
details: Writing `[diarch|E]` in a text shows the word linked to the concept's explanation. The diarch can use special borrowed powers, and gets more of them as the scales of power tip their way.

label: Mundane actions
summary: The game concept Mundane Actions: the liege's interactions that start to cost prestige when the scales of power favor the diarch.
details: Writing `[diarch_affected_actions|E]` in a text shows the word linked to the concept's explanation. The concept lists them, among them revoking a title, retracting a vassal and imprisoning characters.

label: Diarch aptitude
summary: The game concept Diarch Aptitude: how well a diarch carries out each mandate their liege sets.
details: Writing `[diarch_aptitude|E]` in a text shows the word linked to the concept's explanation. Both skills and personality traits count; the concept's example is a greedy diarch who sends less gold under a gold-raising mandate.

label: Loyal (diarch)
summary: The game concept Loyalty of a diarch, in the adjective form "loyal".
details: Writing `[diarch_loyal|E]` in a text shows the word linked to the diarch loyalty explanation, as in vanilla's "not loyal enough to consent to being married off". A diarch's loyalty decides how likely they are to abuse their powers at the expense of their liege or the realm.

label: Diarch loyalty
summary: The game concept Loyalty of a diarch: how likely the diarch is to abuse their powers at the expense of their liege or the realm.
details: Writing `[diarch_loyalty|E]` in a text shows the word linked to the concept's explanation. Clearly loyal diarchs hold back from their borrowed powers, follow their mandate and give up their power willingly.

label: Diarch loyalty
summary: The game concept Loyalty of a diarch, in a fuller form of its name.
details: Writing `[diarch_loyalty_explicit|E]` in a text shows "Diarch Loyalty" linked to the diarch loyalty explanation, where the plain concept shows only "Loyalty". The base game's texts do not use this form. A diarch's loyalty decides how likely they are to abuse their powers.

label: Diarch's
summary: The game concept Diarch in its possessive form.
details: Writing `[diarch_possessive|E]` in a text shows the possessive word linked to the diarch explanation. A diarch is the junior partner who helps their liege run the realm during power sharing.

label: Borrowed power
summary: The game concept Borrowed Power: a special interaction a diarch can use during power sharing.
details: Writing `[diarch_power|E]` in a text shows the word linked to the concept's explanation. These powers copy the liege's own interactions or are other abuses of power, such as revoking titles from fellow vassals or siphoning gold from the liege.
